header.title: A Decade of Learning and Innovation.

body.1: - Arffornia is more than a Minecraft server.
body.2: It's a whole ecosystem combining a {Laravel} website with {MySQL}, an {Electron} game launcher, interconnected server instances with a Velocity proxy, and a scalable {Kubernetes} (k8s) infrastructure for high availability. Built on {Proxmox}-managed virtualization.
body.3: - This 10+ year project has been my playground for learning, innovation, and technical refinement.

blocks.kubernetes: I designed my infrastructure around Kubernetes for scalability and reliability, enabling seamless interconnection of independent modules.
blocks.electron: Cross-Platform Desktop Apps Framework, that I used to create my game launcher on: Windows, Mac and Linux.
blocks.laravel: Backend PHP framework, that I used to create my website and web API using MVC architectural pattern.
blocks.docker: I've extensively used Docker to create independent modules for my k8s.
blocks.github: Automated deployments and test pipelines were built using Github CI/CD, connected to my k8s using ArgoCD.
blocks.java: I develop Forge mods and Spigot/NMS plugins to directly integrate the environment into the game.
blocks.php: I used PHP extensively for the web API and the Laravel website.
blocks.mysql: I used MySQL to manage all my databases.
blocks.typescript: I extensively used TypeScript for developing the game launcher built on Electron.
blocks.proxmox: Manage all my VMs and interconnect them with several physical servers.
blocks.argocd: I built my K8s infra around an ArgoCD controller to achieve deeper integration with the CI/CD pipeline.
blocks.grafana: Have an overview of all my services and create new data by combining other statistics, so that I can anticipate and guide my next choices.

description.1: Arffornia is a Minecraft modded server where players can create technological, magical, and diverse cities, embark on adventures with friends, and share unforgettable moments with the community.
description.2: The 5th season, set to release in a few months, is currently in development and will feature major updates, including a new launcher, an improved website, and the introduction of a progression stage system across various mods.

description.1: The game launcher allows users with just two clicks to login (using Microsoft Account), download and install the game along with all its mods, configure settings, Java version and start playing all in a highly intuitive and user-friendly way on Windows, Mac and Linux.
description.2: Initially developed using JavaFX, I switched to Electron to speed up development and leverage enhanced front-end capabilities using Vue.js. This transition allowed me to create a more modern and visually appealing application, simplifying tasks that would have been complex and time-consuming to achieve with JavaFX.

blocks.java: I develop the previous game launcher with Java & JavaFX.

description.1: To ensure direct visibility on the internet and to centralize my services, such as Account Management, Downloads, API, and more, I developed a website using Laravel. In 2023, I migrated to Laravel to enhance security, expand functionality, and stay up to date with modern web technologies.

The high resource demands of multiple Minecraft server instances and additional services required a highly efficient and robust infrastructure to ensure smooth gameplay. The infrastructure is built around several interconnected physical machines, virtualized with Proxmox, and hosting a Kubernetes (k8s) cluster that runs and monitors all services.
description.2: Above that, I use a Pterodactyl service to manage all Minecraft server instances, with a Velocity Proxy interconnecting them. To enable communication across all services, the Laravel website, featuring a custom API connected to a MySQL database.

description.1: Arffornia ecosystem is built with a modular design, allowing new features and functionalities to be seamlessly integrated through a {philosophy}. To achieve this, I leverage ArgoCD and a GitHub CI/CD pipeline to fully automate deployments. All configurations are managed within a Git repository, ensuring that every change is tested in a dedicated staging environment before being deployed to production. The infrastructure is designed to scale effortlessly based on current server load, dynamically allocating resources during peak usage. In the event of an issue, such as a server instance crash, the corresponding Kubernetes pod automatically initiates a restart, and I am immediately notified to ensure swift resolution.

head.content: Self-hosted internal developer platform: self-service provisioning, GitOps, strict multi-tenancy, running on a private Kubernetes cluster (OpenStack HomeLab).

header.title: Making the cloud invisible to developers.

description.1: CNP is an internal developer platform (IDP) I designed and built as tech lead, with a 6-person team over 5 months (February-July 2026, EPITA SIGL). I carried almost all of the infrastructure: the 4 functional planes, the Kubernetes cluster and its GitOps setup, and the private OpenStack HomeLab.
description.2: The concrete result: a developer, junior or expert, deploys a complete application (Git repo, CI/CD, database, secrets, SSO, DNS) in 3 minutes on their own, without ever getting direct access to the cluster.

context.title: Why build a cloud native platform?

description.1: 4 realities drove our architecture decisions:
description.2: - Productivity & Time-to-Market: self-service deployment in 3 minutes instead of several days, with fast onboarding (under an hour, AI-assisted).
description.3: - Risk mitigation: security applied by default on every project, with strict RBAC (owner / admin / guest).
description.4: - Cost control (FinOps): every team sees what their app actually costs and can set a budget.
description.5: - Governance & auditability: every deployment action is traced (who, what, when) for easy audits, without slowing teams down.
description.6: Give developers autonomy, the company security, and finance teams cost control, all in one platform.

architecture.title: An orchestrator of orchestrators, Git as the source of truth

description.1: The CMP never talks directly to the Kubernetes API to deploy an app. It orchestrates 4 clearly separated functional planes:
description.2: - Control Plane (Next.js + FastAPI): captures the developer's intent and orchestrates tasks through a Saga pattern.
description.3: - Provisioning Plane (Terraform): isolates the context, generates an ephemeral GitHub token, configures Keycloak, Vault and DNS.
description.4: - Delivery Plane (ArgoCD + Helm): continuously syncs the K3s cluster from the app repos.
description.5: - Security & Network Plane (Cilium, Envoy Gateway, Vault): enforces network isolation and authentication on every request.
description.6: Each plane writes its state to Git, which stays the platform's single source of truth: a single commit is enough for a reproducible deployment, with no cluster access and no infra ticket.

security.title: Zero-Trust isolation at the network, identity and secrets layers

description.1: 4 independent security layers, each with its own boundaries:
description.2: - Network: Cilium in default-deny, only intra-project traffic and the Gateway get through.
description.3: - Edge: Envoy Gateway checks the JWT token's groups before it even routes the request.
description.4: - Identity: Keycloak SSO with mandatory MFA from the very first login.
description.5: - Secrets: Vault policy scoped per project, tied to the namespace's Kubernetes Auth role.
description.6: An attempt from one tenant to reach another is blocked by Cilium at the network layer, before it ever reaches the target application.

isolation.title: One Keycloak group, one boundary everywhere

description.1: A project's Keycloak group propagates all the way to the Vault policy, the ArgoCD AppProject and the Grafana organization: a single source of truth for the entire isolation chain.
description.2: 100% of changes are auditable and traced: even legitimate access to one project opens no door into another.

selfservice.title: A path for every skill level, without ever losing anyone

description.1: Every team is an isolated project (Keycloak, Vault, ArgoCD) with clear roles:
description.2: - Project Lead (Owner): creates the project, manages members, tracks their team's deployment costs.
description.3: - Developer (Admin): SSO + MFA, deploys via the catalog or directly through Git, AI assistance through MCP.
description.4: - Guest (Viewer): read-only on the resources they need.
description.5: App templates, identity & SSO, managed database, zero-plaintext secrets, continuous S3 backups and FinOps auto-sleep are all ready from Day-0: nothing improvised in prod.

homelab.title: The HomeLab: a real OpenStack cluster, at my place

description.1: CNP's Kubernetes cluster doesn't run on a public cloud: it runs on a private OpenStack cluster I personally host and administer, at home, electricity bill and subscription included, roughly $200/year all-in.
description.2: OpenStack supports live-migrating a VM from one node to another without interrupting service: that's what let us add RAM or do hardware maintenance without ever taking the platform down.
description.3: The Provisioning Plane stays provider-agnostic (Strategy pattern): the same Terraform model can target this self-hosted K3s cluster as easily as legacy AWS or OpenStack VMs. Work in progress for next semester: extend that independence to AWS and GCP, so we stop depending on a single site.

description.1: A Kubernetes operator I built on my own initiative to automatically shut down non-production environments at night and on weekends, with a one-click manual wake-up. Deployed on most of the platform's non-critical applications.

results.title: 2 real incidents, and a plan for when it breaks

description.1: A heatwave caused the cluster to overload: infrastructure down for ≤1h, fixed by adding RAM and cleaning the cooling airflow.
description.2: A live OpenStack migration was later carried out with zero downtime.
description.3: Dependency we currently accept: a single site at my place, with Bouygues Telecom and EDF as single points of failure. That's exactly what the multi-cloud effort is meant to fix.

2.title: ≤1h
2.description: committed recovery time per incident, thanks to rebuilding from Git via GitOps.

3.description: of changes are auditable and traced, since every deployment goes through a commit.

4.description: cost cut on non-production environments thanks to auto-sleep (Offhours-Guard).

5.description: per node per day internally, about €1/day saved versus an equivalent public cloud setup.

6.title: ~$200/yr
6.description: all-in (electricity + subscription) to host the physical HomeLab.

decisions.title: What we could have done differently, and why we didn't

description.1: - Full GitOps instead of a direct Kubernetes controller: slower to write, but full traceability and the ability to rebuild everything from Git alone won out.
description.2: - Project > Application isolation instead of a plain namespace: one namespace per app would have been technically enough, but didn't match how teams are actually organized.
description.3: - Multi-provider strategy (Strategy pattern) instead of a single provider: hardcoding for K3s would have been simpler short-term, but would have blocked migrating a legacy VM without breaking anything for the developer.

outcome.title: More than a technical tool: a company standard

description.1: - Speed & autonomy: from several days of waiting to 3 minutes, across the whole lifecycle (Day-0 and Day-2).
description.2: - Security & governance: 100% of changes auditable and traced, inside a standardized Zero-Trust framework.
description.3: - Financial control: up to -70% cost on non-production environments.
description.4: We built far more than a technical tool: a real company standard, ready to scale and to integrate tomorrow's innovations (AI/MCP).

head.content: Personal Kubernetes operator that automatically sleeps non-production environments, with real efficiency numbers.

header.title: A Kubernetes operator that only pays for what's used.

description.1: After noticing most of the CNP cluster's non-production environments ran 24/7 for nothing, I built Offhours-Guard on my own initiative: a Kubernetes operator written in Go, with its own OffhoursSchedule CRD.
description.2: A confession: this didn't start as a FinOps project. I mostly wanted to stop myself from coding until stupid o'clock. The default window stops non-prod services from 1am to 5am, far too narrow to be a real energy-saving policy, plenty wide enough to force me to close the laptop. The actual cost benefit came later, once I applied it to every non-production environment on the CNP platform.

1.title: Go
1.description: Written with the standard controller-runtime SDK for Kubernetes operators.

2.title: CRD & Reconciler
2.description: OffhoursSchedule is a real Kubernetes resource: each app declares its sleep and wake schedule as cron + timezone.

3.title: Image & Helm Chart
3.description: Published open source, image and Helm chart shipped continuously through CI.

4.title: GitHub Actions CI
4.description: Build, push and release automated on every change to the project.

how.title: A reconciler that remembers state, not just a cron job

description.1: The reconciler scales deployments down to 0 replicas at the scheduled time, remembering the original replica count so it restores the exact prior state on wake-up, not just a default "1 replica".
description.2: A web dashboard (Tailwind + HTMX) lists every managed app with its state (Active / Asleep), current vs. original replica count and the cron schedule details, with a one-click button to force a wake-up or a manual sleep, auto-refreshing every 15 seconds.

outcome.title: Already deployed, built to go further

description.1: Now deployed on most of the CNP platform's non-critical applications, cutting up to -70% cost on non-production environments and reducing nightly activity from 24/7 to 1h-7h.
description.2: Next step: a recommendation engine, both statistical and AI-assisted, to dynamically suggest better schedules to cluster admins and to users themselves.

outcome.link: See the Cloud Native Platform project →

description.1: A service that's intentionally stopped shouldn't fire an alert as if it had crashed. Offhours-Guard exposes an endpoint that Gatus, CNP's health-check tool, queries instead of the real service.
description.2: During the sleep window, that endpoint directly returns 200 OK with a "SLEEPING (managed by Offhours-Guard)" status. Outside that window, it faithfully proxies the app's real status. Monitoring stays honest, never mistaking a scheduled shutdown for an incident.
